titulo: Quiz — Rules with a price tag
subtitulo: Four streets from the beach, a can of beer, a card machine — and then a bar where the sign isn't in Spanish
introPt: Quiz time. It's late August in Barcelona. Our traveller has walked up from the beach, shirt still in the bag, open can of beer in hand, and a Guàrdia Urbana officer has just clocked her from twenty metres away. Everything that happens next is in this episode. Listen as many times as you like, then answer.
cenario: A tourist walking off the beach is stopped by a city police officer for going shirtless and drinking in the street, pays on the spot by card, then walks into a neighbourhood bar where the barman greets her in Catalan and, two drinks in, asks her what she thinks about independence.

dialogo.es: Buenas tardes. Aquí no se puede ir sin camiseta.
dialogo.pinyin: BWEH-nahs TAR-dehs. ah-KEE noh seh PWEH-dheh eer seen kah-mee-SEH-tah
dialogo.pt: — Good afternoon. You can't go around here with no shirt on.

dialogo.es: Perdón, no lo sabía. Ahora mismo me la pongo.
dialogo.pinyin: pehr-DOHN, noh loh sah-BEE-ah. ah-OH-rah MEES-moh meh lah POHN-goh
dialogo.pt: — Sorry, I didn't know. I'm putting it on right now.

dialogo.es: Vale. Pero la cerveza en la calle tampoco. Eso sí es multa.
dialogo.pinyin: BAH-leh. PEH-roh lah thehr-BEH-thah en lah KAH-yeh tam-POH-koh. EH-soh see es MOOL-tah
dialogo.pt: — Fine. But the beer in the street isn't allowed either. That one is a fine.

dialogo.es: Ciento veinte euros. Y se paga aquí mismo, con tarjeta.
dialogo.pinyin: THYEN-toh BAYN-teh EH-oo-rohs. ee seh PAH-gah ah-KEE MEES-moh, kon tar-KHEH-tah
dialogo.pt: — A hundred and twenty euros. And it's paid right here, by card.

dialogo.es: ¿Me lo puede dar por escrito, por favor?
dialogo.pinyin: meh loh PWEH-dheh dar por ehs-KREE-toh, por fah-BOR
dialogo.pt: — Could you give me that in writing, please?

dialogo.es: Sí, aquí tiene el recibo. Buenas tardes.
dialogo.pinyin: see, ah-KEE TYEH-neh el rreh-THEE-boh. BWEH-nahs TAR-dehs
dialogo.pt: — Yes, here's your receipt. Good afternoon.
— (twenty minutes later, walking into a small bar) Hello.
— Hello! What can I get you two? (the barman — 'os' is vosotros, plural you)

dialogo.es: Sois ingleses, ¿no? ¿Y qué pensáis de todo el lío de la independencia?
dialogo.pinyin: soys een-GLEH-sehs, noh? ee keh pen-SAIS deh TOH-dhoh el LEE-oh deh lah een-deh-pen-DEN-thyah
dialogo.pt: — You're English, right? So what do you make of the whole independence mess?

dialogo.es: Uf. No conozco bien el tema, cuénteme.
dialogo.pinyin: oof. noh koh-NOHTH-koh byen el TEH-mah, KWEN-teh-meh
dialogo.pt: — Oof. I don't really know the subject — tell me about it.

perguntas.pergunta: The officer stops her for two separate things. What are they?
opcoes: Being shirtless in the street, and drinking in the street
Swimming outside the flags, and littering
Sleeping on the beach, and smoking on a terrace
Buying from a street seller, and taking photos of police
perguntas.explica: Two different rules, two different sources: shirtless in a public space is the Barcelona civility ordinance (€120–300, in force since February 2026); the open can is national — the 2015 public security act, €100–600, and up to €1,500 in Barcelona in the wrong zone.

perguntas.pergunta: Her first reaction is the one this episode drills. What does she actually say?
opcoes: Es que en mi país se puede (well, in my country you're allowed to)
Perdón, no lo sabía. Ahora mismo me la pongo (sorry, I didn't know — I'm putting it on right now)
No hablo español (I don't speak Spanish)
¿Y usted quién es? (and who are you?)
perguntas.explica: Regret plus immediate action: 'no lo sabía' + 'ahora mismo', while the shirt actually goes on. An officer watching the problem being fixed usually walks away. An officer being lectured does not.

perguntas.pergunta: He says the fine is 'ciento veinte euros'. How much is that — and watch out, this is the sound Spain makes that Latin America doesn't.
perguntas.explica: Ciento veinte = 120. That 'th' at the start of ciento is the distinción — the c before e or i is the 'th' of 'think'. It's the same sound that separates cincuenta (50) from sesenta (60) on every bill you'll be handed.

perguntas.pergunta: 'Se paga aquí mismo, con tarjeta.' Why is that line the single most up-to-date fact in this episode?
opcoes: Because Spanish police only take cash
Because Barcelona's ordinance now makes non-residents pay on the spot, and the Guàrdia Urbana carries card machines
Because tourists get a 50% discount if they pay immediately
Because the fine is voided if you have no card on you
perguntas.explica: The old folk wisdom — 'they'll never chase a tourist for it' — died in February 2026. Collection used to be near zero once you'd flown home, so the new ordinance obliges non-residents to pay immediately and the officers now carry terminals.

perguntas.pergunta: She asks for it 'por escrito'. Why bother, once she's already paid?
opcoes: It's required by law before you can pay
It gets the amount reduced
The receipt is her only proof she paid, if the same fine turns up again later
It lets her appeal automatically
perguntas.explica: '¿Me lo puede dar por escrito, por favor?' is the same button you press at the hire-car counter. Anything you've paid or agreed to, get on paper — it costs one sentence and it is the only thing you can show later.

perguntas.pergunta: She walks into the bar and says 'Bon dia' instead of 'Buenos días'. What's going on?
opcoes: It's Catalan — a separate language, and a two-second courtesy that visibly changes the service
It's Spanish with a Barcelona accent
It's obligatory in Catalonia and you can be fined for using Spanish
It's Basque
perguntas.explica: Catalan is a language in its own right, not a dialect or an accent. You will never be required to use it — everyone switches to Spanish the moment they hear your accent — but 'bon dia' on the way in and 'adéu' on the way out cost you nothing and land every time.

perguntas.pergunta: The barman asks 'qué os pongo?' and later 'qué pensáis?'. What should you notice about those?
opcoes: They're Catalan words
They're vosotros — the plural 'you' that only exists in Spain, and you'll be on the receiving end of it constantly
They're formal usted forms
They're grammatical mistakes
perguntas.explica: As a couple or a group you are always the target of vosotros and almost never the producer of it. Put it in your ear, not your mouth: '¿qué os pongo?', '¿habéis reservado?', '¿de dónde sois?' — recognise those three and you've covered most of what a pair of travellers ever gets asked.

perguntas.pergunta: The barman asks her straight out what she thinks about Catalan independence. What's the risk, and what's the right move?
opcoes: It's legally dangerous — refuse to answer and leave
No legal risk at all, but real social cost — hand the floor back with 'No conozco bien el tema, cuénteme'
Say you support independence, since he brought it up in Catalan
Say you support both sides equally
perguntas.explica: Zero legal exposure — Spain argues about this openly every week. The cost is purely social. Don't guess his side from the fact he greeted you in Catalan (Catalan speakers have polled majority-against independence), don't opine, ask. And with someone your own age it's 'cuéntame' — tú is the Spanish default; save 'cuénteme' for the older man, the uniform and the formal counter.
